analysis.one_liner: Strengthens penalties and lawsuits for unequal pay between men and women and makes large employers report pay data by sex and race.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 95 House cosponsors but never got a hearing or a vote; it died in committee when the 105th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give women who are paid less than men for equal work stronger tools to fight back: new protection against being punished for discussing wages, bigger damages in lawsuits, and the right to sue as a class. It would also require employers with 100 or more workers to report pay data by race, sex, and national origin to the EEOC, and would fund more enforcement and public education on pay gaps.
analysis.who_benefits: Women who are paid less than men for jobs requiring equal skill, effort, and responsibility would gain stronger legal remedies, including compensatory and punitive damages, class-action rights, expert fees, and protection from being fired or punished for asking about or discussing wages. Workers at large employers would also gain from the pay data the EEOC collects, which the bill directs it to analyze by race, sex, and national origin.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Women paid less than male coworkers

how_it_helps.text: It adds a retaliation ban to the Equal Pay Act, making it illegal for an employer to punish a worker for inquiring about, discussing, or disclosing wages, so workers can find out whether they are being underpaid.
It lets workers who win equal-pay cases recover compensatory and punitive damages, not just lost wages, and lets courts order employers to pay expert fees.
It explicitly allows sex-based pay discrimination cases to be brought as class actions, so underpaid workers can sue together instead of one at a time.

It requires employers with 100 or more employees to report pay information analyzed by race, sex, and national origin to the EEOC, which would make pay gaps visible to enforcers without exposing individual workers.
It funds training, research, voluntary pay guidelines, and a national summit on eliminating pay disparities between men and women.

analysis.who_pays: Employers who pay unequal wages would bear the cost of new compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and higher penalties; employers with 100 or more employees would bear the cost of collecting and submitting payroll data by race, sex, and national origin to the EEOC; taxpayers would fund the new appropriations to the EEOC, OFCCP, and Labor Department.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large employers facing damages and reporting

drawbacks.text: The bill exposes employers to punitive damages and class actions, and an honest supporter would acknowledge that some of that added cost falls on businesses whose pay practices were already lawful, and may be passed to consumers or workers.
Employers with 100 or more employees would face a new administrative burden to collect and submit payroll records analyzed by race, sex, and national origin each year.
Parts of the bill are symbolic or administrative, including a national award medal and a $1 million authorization for outreach, which do not directly change any worker's paycheck.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefits are real and targeted: workers who discuss wages would gain legal protection, and workers who win equal-pay cases would gain meaningful damages and the option to sue as a class, which changes the practical math of bringing a claim. The costs are compliance and litigation exposure for employers, concentrated on businesses that pay unequally but spread to some that do not, plus about $48 million in authorized spending. The pay-data reporting provision is the most consequential piece, because gaps that are invisible to the EEOC today would become enforceable records. On balance the bill's benefits to workers outweigh its costs, though the award medal and summit provisions are largely symbolic.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee and then in two subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 105th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rosa DeLauro introduced the bill on June 24, 1997 with Eleanor Holmes Norton and Dick Gephardt as original cosponsors, and it was referred to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce the same day.
The committee sent it to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations and the Subcommittee on Workforce Protections on July 22, 1997.
The bill attracted 95 cosponsors, 94 Democrats and 1 Independent, but no further action was recorded and the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 without a hearing or a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who would have faced expanded pay-discrimination liability and the new payroll reporting requirement are better off, because the bill never advanced beyond referral and no vote was ever taken.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers who would have faced new liability

against.what_they_did: Received the referral, then assigned it to two subcommittees, and never scheduled a markup or reported the bill to the floor before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no party split appears in the record; the 95 cosponsors were 94 Democrats and 1 Independent, and no Republican signed on.

industries.industry: Large private employers (100 or more employees)
industries.note: The bill would subject employers to compensatory and punitive damages, class actions, and expert fees for unequal pay, and would require those with 100 or more employees to file pay reports broken down by race, sex, and national origin. These are the direct compliance and litigation costs the bill creates.

industries.industry: Federal civil rights enforcement agencies (EEOC, OFCCP)
industries.note: The bill authorizes $36 million in new funds for the EEOC and $10 million for OFCCP and directs new pay-data reporting and training duties to them, expanding their enforcement role. Whether this serves ordinary workers depends on how aggressively the agencies enforce.

By allowing class actions and punitive damages for sex-based pay discrimination, the bill would generate more employment litigation, which is work for defense firms and cost for employers. Some of that litigation is exactly what the bill intends to deter unequal pay with.
